## Mathematical notation

A mathematical model is proposed that describes the feature table counts obtained after quality filtering of the data obtained from an NGS sequencing process. A formal notation of the results helps to identify and compare the overall and marginal summary statistics and to choose the most appropriate analysis tool, data transform or  normalization domain, based on the scope of the analysis required, thus easing the reproducibility data processing utcomes. Furthermore, a statistical characterization is provided to describe algorithms that overcome or compensate for the biases introduced by the inference process applied to the compositional data, thus facilitating the setup of the workflow and therefore the reproducibility of the analyses. A particular emphasis is given to missing data that are explicitly indicated as *NA*. Within this notation the ratio, rank, logarithmic ratio, reference data frame and sampling fraction are defined.

## Missing data management {#sec:MissData}

Sparsity of NGS data is known to be critical issue for managing benchmarking tools. The sparsity is due, however, to the attribution of zeros to the missing features. In fact, if a single sample is sequenced, thus all features counts are non-null since the instrument cannot reveal what is not sequenced. If more than one sample is considered in a feature table, thus some characteristics may be only in a sample while missing in at least one of the others. Each sample contributes to the ecosystem composition with its own feature and the union of samples defines the entire set of features used for benchmarking. When target sequencing is used, the feature set is the microbiome, when RNA-seq is used the feature set is genes. GIUSTIFICARE I MISSING DATA CON BIBLIO. In this paper not available (*NA*) data  are indicated with "-" in the proposed model of the feature table and the most pertinent  pseudo-count, "0", "1" or whatever, is added to the table elements, if appropriate or necessary based on the type of analysis required. In fact, ignoring *NA* in the evaluation of summary statistics is equivalent to excluding missing features from the composition and evaluating the sample as if it were sequenced alone. Using pseudocounting instead allows missing features to be included in the compositional evaluation but may influence the value of some of the summary statistics compared to ignoring *NA*. The difference between the results is often considered a bias, but in reality the addition of the pseudocunt serves the purposes of the analysis. For example, ignoring *NA* or adding the pseudocount "0" to all feature counts, the values of the sample proportions do not change but the average values of the counts are affected more significantly the greater the number of *NA*, i.e. of zeros. Furthermore, considering statistics on log-transformed data, the pseudocunt "0" is not allowed and the value "1" is generally inserted instead. Also in this case the sample average values are more altered the greater the number of missing data, i.e. of ones, compared to the case of ignoring the *NA*.

The two statistics, without and with pseudocount,  refer to completely different feature compositions that must be considered specifically and therefore their difference cannot be classified as bias.


## NGS feature table {#Sec:TableAL}

The sequencing outcome of a set of samples, $\mathbf{S}=\{S_1,...,S_S\}$, is described by a feature table, **A**, i.e. a table with the counts of each feature detected in each sample after appropriate quality filtering of raw reads. When taxonomies present hierarchical structure, the feature table can be clustered based on the taxonomic level, if required by the specific analysis, and thus **$\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}$** indicates the table clustered at level $L$ where each feature index is labeled with a subscript '$\text{@}L$'. A template representation of such a table is given in Fig. \@ref(fig:FeatTab).

Aggiungere Summary stats and missing data treatment !!!

\begin{figure}[ht]
\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth]{./Tables/TableModel.png} \caption{\label{fig:FeatTab}Table**$\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}$**: representation of a feature table at taxonomic level $L$.}\label{fig:FeatTab}
\end{figure}


Elements of the feature table at level $L$, $a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}$, represent the observed absolute abundance of the $i-th$ feature at level $L$, $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$, in the $j-th$ sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{_j}}$, i.e. is the frequency of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ in $S_{\textcolor{gray}{_j}}$.  The $i-th$ row is a row vector with $S$ elements represented by
<!-- $\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[i,]=[a(i_{\text{@}L},1),...,a(i_{\text{@}L},j),...,a(i_{\text{@}L},S)]$ -->
$\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[i_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}},]=\left[a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},1)}}, \dots, a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}, \dots, a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},S)}}\right].$
The $j-th$ column is a  vector with $\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}$ elements representd by $\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,j]=[a_{\textcolor{gray}{(1,j)}},...,a{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}},...,a_{\textcolor{gray}{(\widehat{F}_{\text{@}L},j)}}]^T$. 


The number of type of observed features at taxonomic level $L$ in the table $\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}$ is indicated with $\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}$ and is an estimate of the richness of sequenced samples, $F_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}$, whose accuracy is related both to  the sequencing depth and to the taxonomies distribution, as detailed below. 

After the quality filtering process, the set of sequenced features at taxonomic level $L$ defines the observed microbiome, which is indicated with 
<!-- $\mathbf{F_{@L}}$, has richness equal to $F_{@L}$ and is formed by the set of sequenced features $F[i_{@L}]$ with index $i_{@L}=1_{@L},2_{@L},...,F_{@L}$, i.e. -->
$\mathbf{\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}}=[F_{\textcolor{gray}{(1_{@L})}},F_{\textcolor{gray}{(2_{@L})}},...,F_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{@L})}},...,F_{\textcolor{gray}{(\widehat{F}_{@L})}}]^T$, being $F(i_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}})$ the $i_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}$-th taxon at level $L$ and $i_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}=1_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}},2_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}},...,\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}$ the integer indexes up to the observed sample richness, $\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}$. 

Last column of Table in Fig. \@ref(fig:FeatTab) summarizes the number of reads, $R_{\textcolor{gray}{({i_{\text{@}L},T)}}}$, recorded for each feature $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ in the considered set of samples $\mathbf{S}$ and represents the absolute abundance in the sequenced ecosystem. It should be noted that the minimum observed count in the whole sequencing is equal to 1, i.e. $R_{\textcolor{gray}{({i_{\text{@}L}},T)}} > 0$ for all features at whatever taxonomic level.

Due to the hierarchical structure of the taxonomic database, the feature abundances from SV to phylum are columnwise sorted in ascending order, i.e. $a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{@SV},j)}} \le  a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{6},j)}} \le a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{@5},j)}}  \le ... \le a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{@1},j)}}]$ for each $j$. The sample sequence depth, that for a 16S sequencing is the total number of SVs, is given by $R_{\textcolor{gray}{(T,j)}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\widehat{F}}{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{@L},j)}}}$ and represents the so called sample library size which is used to estimate the relative abundance of each feature. Last line of the table shows the sequencing depth for each sample. 

It is worth to recall that when counts within a biological sample is obtained by sequencing platforms, the number of DNA molecules of the analyzed ecosystem (also referred to as total sample microbial load) are sequenced after a random subsampling [@gloor2017microbiome]. It follows that the instrument detects the most probable features, together to some rares, respecting their mutual compositional relationships. Moreover, since the sequenced number of counts recorded is constrained by the total library size, absolute observed abundances depends on chemistry of the assay and not the input material and thus is arbitrary [@quinn2018understanding].  Quality filtering applied  to raw data after sequencing is a further subsampling process needed for removing reads mostly affected by random errors accumulated in the sample processing workflow. 
<!-- When more than one samples are sequenced simultaneously, barcodes are inserted in order to identify a-posteriorir eads attaining to each sample and the sampling process is run as as the in the instrument is present only one sample. It follows that abundance of features present in the whole sequencing respect their mutual proportions and thus, once features are assigned to each sample, also the samples library sizes represent the abundance of the samples and respct mutual proprtions.   -->
When more than one samples are sequenced simultaneously, barcodes are inserted into the DNA to subsequently identify the sample they belong to, and the sequencing process is performed as if there were a single sample. It follows that the abundance of features present in the entire sequencing respects mutual composition without considering the sample of origin. Once features are reassigned to each sample, the abundance in each sample is redistributed based on the barcodes. Therefore the size of the sample library, $R_{\textcolor{gray}{(T,j)}}$, represents the abundance in each sample, and since compositions among samples are respected, thus ratios between two library sizes respect the ratio between the corresponding samples microbial loads. See section \@ref(sec:BayesTh) for formal proof.
<!-- the result of DNA sequencing is a subsampling of the molecules of the analyzed ecosystem which is performed randomly [@gloor2017microbiome]. -->  
 
Since the absolute counts are not related to the original number of molecules of the biological samples, some sort of normalization is necessary (with respect to a summary statistic, rarefaction or otherwise), and particular attention must also be paid to the normalization domain (with respect to the features, to samples or sequencing) most appropriate to apply as detailed in the section \@ref(sec:Normalization). In any case, whatever the normalization method or the normalization domain, by assuming the feature counts follow a binomial distribution as decribed in sec. \@ref(sec:BinMod), an unbiased estimator of the proportion of the $i_{\textcolor{gray}{@L}}$-th taxon is given by the absolute count normalized to the corresponding domain library size. Thus, the precision of sample proportional abundance estimates is governed by the library size value [@gloor2017microbiome].



## Normalization and summary domains {#sec:Normalization}

The major  domains across which the absolute abundance feature table $\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}$ can be summarized and/or normalized are: 

- within-sample (across-features): summary stats and normalization factors are evaluated on each column;
- across-samples (within-features): summary stats and normalization factors are evaluated on each row;
- whole-table: summary stats and normalization factors are evaluated acroos the whole table;
- across-groups (within/across-samples within-across-features): summary stats and normalization factors are evaluated in subgroups of samples or features.

These domains are closely related to each other, marginal statistics of each normalized table can be used to summarize an entire sequencing or its subgroups, to determine cluster signatures based on feature abundances, and to compare sample composition of clusters. Since the data are compositional, the chosen  normalization method affects the summary statistics and therefore must be carefully selected based on the purposes of the analyses.
Figure \@ref(fig:Norm) shows as an example the normalization of the abundance to the total sum of reads that can be evaluated in each of the three domains indicated above. The use of each of these sums as a normalization factor to the absolute abundance value $a(i_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@L}}},j)$, defines the estimate of a corresponding proportion described below:

- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|j)}}$ is the within-sample proportion of $F{{\textcolor{gray}i_{\text{@}L}}}$ that is probability that a sequenced read, known to be in sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$, is the feature $F{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$; the corresponding estimate is $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|j)}}=a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}/R_{\textcolor{gray}{(T,j)}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{(j|i_{\text{@}L})}}$ is the across-sample proportion of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ that is the the probability that a read, identified as $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$, is in the sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$; the corresponding estimate is $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{(j|i_{\text{@}L})}}=a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}/R_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},T)}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_(\text{@L},j)}}$ is the proportion of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$  evaluated over the entire table that is the probability that  the read is the feature $F{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ and is in sample $S_j$; the corresponding estimate is $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}=a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}/R_{\textcolor{gray}{(T,T)}}$.

- Aggiungere le probabilità marginali, la prevalenza (solo quando si confrontano campioni !), statistiche marginali (AM,GM)

<!-- These three conditional probabilities are related as follows: $p(i_{\text{@}L},j)=p(i_{\text{@}L}|j)p(j)=p(j|i_{\text{@}L})p(i_{\text{@}L})$, where $p(j)$ and $p(i_{\text{@}L})$ are the probabilities that a read is in $S_j$ and that it is  $F(i_{\text{@}L})$, respectively. -->


\begin{figure}[ht]
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{./Tables/Norm.png} \caption{\label{fig:FeatTab}Table $\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}$: normalization with respect to each sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$, to each feature $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$, and to the whole sequencing.}\label{fig:Norm}
\end{figure}


Similarly, further normalization methods use summary statistics other than the total sum of readings, such as arithmetic mean, geometric mean, abundance of a presumed invariant feature, rarefaction, ... Such statistics are applicable to absolute abundances or their transformations and can be evaluated in each of the normalization domains in the same way as for proportions. The choice of domain depends on purposes of the required analysis.

In this paper, a special attention is given the abundance expressed as clr.

$\sum_{i_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}=1}^{F_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}|j}}}=1=\frac{1}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,j}}}\sum_{i_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}=1}^{F_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}}$

# Bayes theorem {#sec:BayesTh}

It is known that joint and conditional probabilities of two independent events $i$ and $j$ are related by the following relationship:
<!-- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}=p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}=p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ -->
\begin{equation} \label{eq:BayesTh}
p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}=p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}=p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}
\end{equation}

In this article, a statistical model for NGS sequencing is proposed in order to manage the compositional outcomes with appropriate mathematical tools and to propose processing algorithms aemphasizing workflows independent of software programming languages. It is worth mentioning that, after the sequencing process, the $\widehat{F}$ observed reads are processed with the aim of recovering information both on the composition in individual samples and on comparisons of compositions among samples. Since NGS instruments sequence a single compound obtained by multiplexing together randomly selected and barcoded DNA fragments within each sample, after sequencing, each read must be identified with a feature $F_{i}$ among those available in the selected reference database and must also be assigned to the original sample, i.e. $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$. In this context, event $i$ is the identification of a read with the feature $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ available in a reference database.  The event $j$ corresponds to the recognition of a read as belonging to the sequenced sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$.  Both events are independent of each other since, once sequencing has been carried out, the identification of a read with a feature does not influence its belonging to the sample which is instead guaranteed by the sample barcode; furthermore, the inclusion of a read in a sample does not impact on the identification of the characteristic which is rather linked to the reference database. Thus, the joint, conditional and marginal probabilities have the following meanings:

- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}$ is the joint events probability: the probability that a sequenced read belongs to $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ and that is also identified as $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ is the marginal probability of $j$: the probability that a sequenced read belongs to $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ is the marginal probability of $i$: the probability that a sequenced read is identified as $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}$ is the probability of $i$ conditioned to $j$:  the probability that a sequenced read belonging to $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ is $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$.
- $p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}$ is the probability of $j$ conditioned to $i$: the probability that a sequenced read is identified as $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ belongs to $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$.

Considering the entire sequencing of the single compound obtained by multiplexing samples, total counts $R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,T}}$ is fixed by the instrument while feature counts $R_{\textcolor{gray}{i,T}}$, with $i=1,....,\widehat{F}$, respect mutual composition since the instrument randomly read DNA fragments. It follows that after the sequencing process only relative abundances make sense, i.e. proportions or ratios between absolute counts. In this paper a Dirichlet-Multinomial model is assumed for each count (see section \@ref(sec:DMMod)) and thus $$\mathbf{R}_{\textcolor{gray}{i,T}}=[R_{\textcolor{gray}{1,T}},...,R_{\textcolor{gray}{i,T}},...,R_{\textcolor{gray}{\widehat{F},T}}]^T\sim \text{DirMult}(R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,T}}, \boldsymbol{\alpha})$$ with the probability vector $\mathbf{p}=[p_{\textcolor{gray}{1}},...,p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}},...,p_{\textcolor{gray}{\widehat{F}}}]^T$ is derived from a $\rm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ distribution. 
<!-- Vector $\mathbf{\alpha}$ can be viewed as a pseudocount catches prior assumptions about the distribution of features and , i.e. counts of each feature that describe the sequencing, according to the prior probabilities, before the actual data is collected. -->
The vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ can be thought of as a pseudocount describing the distribution of features, according to prior probabilities $\mathbf{p}$, before the actual data is collected. Thus $\mathbf{p}$ is the expected value of sample proportions,$\mathbf{\widehat{p}}$, of sequenced features and, in particular:

- $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}=\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,T}}}$ is the of proportion of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ in sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ evaluated over the entire sequencing; 
- $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}=\frac{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,j}}}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,T}}}$ is the proportion of features in sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ evaluated over the entire sequencing;
- $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}=\frac{R_{\textcolor{gray}{i,T}}}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,T}}}$ is the proportion of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ evaluated over the entire sequencing; 
- $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}=\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,j}}}$ is the proportion of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$ evaluated within sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ ;
- $\widehat{p}_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}=\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}}{R_{\textcolor{gray}{i,T}}}$ is the proportion of features in $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ evaluated among the total counts of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$.

<!-- However, given appropriate prior knowledge, the sum should be adjusted in proportion to the expectation that the prior probabilities should be considered correct, despite evidence to the contrary -->

Considering two features, $i$ and $m$, two samples, $j$ and $k$, the ratios between joint probabilities $p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}$ and $p_{\textcolor{gray}{m,j}}$, the following identities reults:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:Ratiosiminj}
\frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{m,j}}}= \frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{m|j}}}=\frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|m}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{m}}}
\end{equation}



\begin{equation} \label{eq:Ratiosjkofi}
\frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,j}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i,k}}}= \frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{j|i}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{k|i}}}=\frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|j}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i|k}}p_{\textcolor{gray}{k}}}
\end{equation}

Eq. \@ref(eq:Ratiosiminj) asserts  that considering two features $i$ and $m$ within a single sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$, the ratio of proportions evaluated across the entire sequencing is equal to the ratio of proportions evaluated within the sample. On the other hand, when the proportions of individual features present in Sj are evaluated in all samples, in order for their ratio to be equal to the ratio of the proportions evaluated in the entire sequencing, they must be weighted by the ratio between proportions of the corresponding features evaluated in the entire sequencing  

Analogously, eq. \@ref(eq:Ratiosjkofi) states that considering feature $i$ that is present in two samples, $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ and $S_{\textcolor{gray}{k}}$, the ratio of proportions evaluated across the entire sequencing is equal to the ratio between the two samples of the  proportions evaluated among the total counts of $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}$. On the other hand, when the proportions of the features present in the two samples  are evaluated within each sample counts, in order for their ratio to be equal to the ratio of the proportions evaluated in the entire sequencing, they must be weighted by the corresponding sample proportion of features evaluated in the entire sequencing. It should be noticed that the last weight disappears if rarefaction is applied to the samples, since it guarantees the same weight to all samples and thus $\frac{p_{\textcolor{gray}{i}}}{p_{\textcolor{gray}{k}}}=1$ holds true.



## Differential samples abundance

Differential clr abundance of feature $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ between samples $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ and $S_{\textcolor{gray}{k}}$ uses the within-sample abundances and can be evaluated as:

\begin{equation} \label{eq:ClrDiff}
\widehat{\rm{clr}}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|j)}}-\widehat{\rm{clr}}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|k)}} = \log\Big(\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}}{G(\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,j])}\Big)- \log\Big(\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},k)}}}{G(\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,k)}\Big)
\end{equation}

By using the logarithm properties and ....., it results that clr-based differential abundance is the clr evaluated on the abundance ratios as reported in eq. \@ref(eq:ClrDiff).

\begin{equation} \label{eq:ClrDiff}
\widehat{\rm{clr}}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|j)}}-\widehat{\rm{clr}}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|k)}} = \log\Big(\frac{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j)}}}{a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},k)}}}\Big) - \log\Big(G\big(\frac{\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,j])}{\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,k]}\big)\Big)=\widehat{\rm{clr}}_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L}|\frac{j}{k})}}
\end{equation}

<!-- is equal to the clr of feature $F_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}}}$ conditioned to the sample $S_{\textcolor{gray}{j}}$ whose abundances, however, are normalized element by element to those in  $S_{\textcolor{gray}{k}}$.  -->
Being the clr an asymptotic unbiased estimator, thus the CLR-based differential abundance approaches the CLR of the ratio of sample abundances as sequencing depth increases.
<!-- and it equals the log-fold change of samples abundances minus the log-fold change of samples geometric means. If the two GM are equal thus difference between clr represent an unbiased estimate of the of lfc. -->
Since 

 
 
 


<!-- $=  $ -->

<!-- $ -\frac{1-p_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}|j}}}{2p_{\textcolor{gray}{i_{\text{@}L}|j}}R_{\textcolor{gray}{T,j}}}}\Big)\rightarrow \frac{1}{\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}\sum_{i_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}=1}^{\widehat{F}_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}{\log(a_{\textcolor{gray}{(i_{\text{@}L},j})})}=\log(G(\mathbf{A_{\textcolor{gray}{\text{@}L}}}[,j])$ -->
 It follows that differential analysis of abundances between samples requires some kind of normalization. ###***



## Features ranking

In order to benchmark samples based on features abundance, the clr is the only appropriate summary statistics.

$\log G\Big(\frac{\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[i_{\text{@}L},])}{\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[m_{\text{@}L},]}\Big)=\log G\Big(\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[\frac{i_{\text{@}L}}{m_{\text{@}L}},]\Big)$

$E\big\{\log(G(\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[i_{\text{@}L},])\big\}= E\big\{\frac{1}{S}\sum_{j=1}^{S}{\log(a(i_{\text{@}L},j))}\big\} \simeq \frac{1}{S}\sum_{j=1}^{S}{\Big(\log(p_{j|i_{\text{@}L}}R_{i_{\text{@}L}T})-\frac{1-p_{j|i_{\text{@}L}}}{2p_{j|i_{\text{@}L}}R_{i_{\text{@}L}T}}}\Big)\rightarrow \frac{1}{S}\sum_{j=1}^{S}{\log(a_{i_{\text{@}L},j})}=\log(G(\mathbf{A_{\text{@}L}}[i_{\text{@}L},])$

<!-- After the quality filtering process, the the set of sequenced features at taxonomic level $L$ defines the microbiome, which is indicated with  -->
<!-- <!-- $\mathbf{F_{@L}}$, has richness equal to $F_{@L}$ and is formed by the set of sequenced features $F[i_{@L}]$ with index $i_{@L}=1_{@L},2_{@L},...,F_{@L}$, i.e. --> -->
<!-- $\mathbf{F_{@L}}=[F[1_{@L}],F[2_{@L}],...F[i_{@L}],...,F[F_{@L}]]^T$, being $F[i_{@L}]$ the $i_{@L}$-th taxon at level $L$ and $i_{@L}=1_{@L},2_{@L},...,F_{@L}$ the integer indexes up to the sample richness, $F_{@L}$. The absolute observed abundance of each feature is $a[i_{@L}]$ and since we are analyzing the microbiome of a single sample, the minimum observed count is equal to 1, i.e. $a[i_{@L}]>0$ for all features at whatever taxonomic level. Due to the hierarchical structure of the taxonomic database, the feature abundances from SV to phylum are sorted in ascending order, i.e. $a[i_{@SV}] \le  a[i_{@6}] \le a[i_{@5}]  \le ... \le a[i_{@1}]]$. The sample sequence depth, that for a 16S sequencing is the total number of SVs, is given by $R_T=\sum_{i_{@L}=1}^{F_{@L}}{a[i_{@L}]}$ and represents the so called library size which is used to evaluate the relative abundance of each feature. Assuming the feature counts follow a binomial distribution, an unbiased estimator of the proportion of the $i_{@L}$-th taxon is the corresponding absolute count normalized to the library size, i.e. $\hat{p}[i_{@L}]=a[i_{@L}]/R_T$.   -->

It is worth to recall that also in the situation described in this section when only one sample is sequenced by the instrument, the number of DNA molecules of the analyzed ecosystem (also referred to as total microbial load, $A_{@L|j}$) are randomly subsampled and then sequenced [@gloor2017microbiome].
<!-- the result of DNA sequencing is a subsampling of the molecules of the analyzed ecosystem which is performed randomly [@gloor2017microbiome]. --> It follows that the instrument detects the most probable features, together to some rares, respecting their mutual compositional relationships, and that the precision of their proportional abundance estimate is governed by the library size value, $R_T$  [@gloor2017microbiome].
Since the minimum sample proportion in the sample is a positive value, without delving into the tricky details involved in estimating the confidence interval of the binomial proportion, we use the "extended rule of three"  [@hanley1983if] to infer, with a confidence equal to $(1-\alpha)\%$, the value of the smallest taxon proportion that could be sequenced, i.e. the taxonomy sequencing sensitivity. This approach is described in Fig.\ref{FigCI} and evaluates the  upper bound, $p_u$, of the $(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval (CI) for the binomial proportion $p$ when no event is detected in $R_T$ reads, i.e. the feature has zero counts. It results that $p_u(\alpha)=-\log(\alpha)/R_T$ gives a highly accurate estimate of the $(1-\alpha)\%$CI upper bound when a large number of trials are available [@jovanovic1997look], such as in the sequencing field, and represents the largest value of the proportion of rares that is compatible with the observed result $0/R_T$ at a confidence level of at least $(1-\alpha)\%$. 

<!-- ![Upper bound of the binomial $(1-\alpha)\%$CI: the "extended rule of three" approach. Indicating with X a Binomial random variable with parameters $p$ and $R_T$, the upper bound $p_u(\alpha)$ is evaluated by solving $Pr\{X=0|R_T,p\} \ge \alpha$ for $p$. Features with proportions smaller than $p_u(\alpha)$ are cyan emphasized and present a probability at least equal to $\alpha\%$ of not being sequenced. Proportions of features counted for $n$ times in $R_T$ reads are estimated with $\hat{p}=n/R_T$ (red ticks).   \label{FigCI}](./Tables/FigCI.jpg "a title") -->


Thus, considering a confidence level equal to $(1-\alpha)\%$, features not sampled with $R_T$ reads present a proportion value smaller than  $p_u(\alpha)$  while features with at least 1 observation have a proportion value greater than $p_u(\alpha)$ .

<!-- Thus, for each $R_T$, features with proportion value smaller than  $p_u(\alpha)$ have a probability at least equal to $\alpha\%$  of not being sequenced and features characterized by a proportion value largest than $p_u(\alpha)$ have an observed absolute abundance at least equal to 1 with a probability equal to $(1-\alpha)\%$.  -->

It follows that the smallest sample proportion greater than $p_u(\alpha)$ is the taxonomy sensitivity of the sequencing, $sens(\alpha)$, corresponding to a confidence $(1-\alpha)\%$ and that the minimum number of counts that guarantees an estimated proportion greater than $p_u(\alpha)$ is $n_u(\alpha) = \lceil (-\log(\alpha)) \rceil$, where the operator $\lceil \cdot \rceil$ indicates the smallest integer greater than its argument. Thus, taxonomy sensitivity of the sequencing process is given by  
$sens(\alpha)=n_u(\alpha)/R_T$, depends on the library size and is independent of the taxonomy level.
<!-- that have a probability of not being sequenced equal to  $(1-\alpha)\%$ due to limits of the library size. -->

<!-- DECISIONE SU QUALE LIVELLO LAVORARE!!! perchè nu è indipendente da L -->

It should be noted that features with observed sample counts less than $n_u(\alpha)$ are the rare ones and are randomly sampled from the ecosystem according to the constraints imposed by $R_T$.
<!-- with confidence $(1-\alpha)\%$.  -->
The greater the number of reads, the greater the resolution of the taxonomic frequency, i.e. smaller $sens(\alpha)$.

It follows that parameters depending on $R_T$ are $sens(\alpha)$, $\hat{p}$ and $F_{@L}$.



```{r ExtendedRuleThree}
R_T<-c(1000,1000,1000,1000,10000,10000,10000,10000,100000,10000,100000,100000)
#R_T<-rep(seq(1000:1000:10000),3)
alpha<-c(0.05,0.01,0.001,0.0001,0.05,0.01,0.001,0.0001,0.05,0.01,0.001,0.0001)
RuleOf<-round(-log(alpha),digits = 1)
pu<- -log(alpha)/R_T
nu<-(ceiling(RuleOf))

TabRuleOf <-  data.frame(R_T,alpha,RuleOf,pu,nu)%>%
  arrange(R_T)

TabRuleOf<-TabRuleOf%>%
  mutate(R_T=format(R_T, scientific = FALSE))%>%
  mutate(pu=format(pu, scientific = TRUE,digits = 2))%>%
#  mutate(pu=format(pu*100, scientific = TRUE,digits = 2))%>%
  mutate(R_T=as.character(R_T),alpha=as.character(alpha),RuleOf=as.character(RuleOf),pu=as.character(pu),nu=as.character(nu))
TabRuleOfCaption="TabCap"
```

# Parameters of samples in group

When a group of $S$ samples is available, parameters characterizing the $j-th$ sample have the subscript $j$, as indicated in Table\@ref(tab:TabSamplesParameters). The microbiome  $\mathbf{F_{@L}}$ refers to all sequenced samples and the absolute observed abundance of the $i_{@L}$-th feature in the $j-th$ sample, $a[i_{@L},j]$, admits the zero value, i.e. all features belongs to at least one sample but not all samples may present all features.  The sample sequence depth is given by $R_{T|j}=\sum_{i_{@L}=1}^{F_{@L}}{a[i_{@L},j]}$ and represents the sample library size which is used to estimate the relative abundance of each feature in the sample, $\hat{p}_{i@L|j}=a_{i@L|j}/R_{T|j}$.  When samples come from the same ecosystem, the total microbial load, $A_{@L|j}$, is a characteristic common to all samples of the group and is independent on $j$. 
Since high throughput sequencing processes many samples at the same time, also the sample proportion of each feature within the whole sequencing, $\hat{p}_{i,j}$ is a parameter to be considered for the evaluation of the quality of the sequecing.

## Microbiome

The microbiome of a sample can be specified and analyzed for each taxonomic level up to the species or sequence variant (SV) level. Taxonomy abundances and average values perform differently based on the taxonomic level, $L$, that is a parameter that should be also considered for evaluating the biodiversity degree of a sample or an ecosystem or the differences between diversity of groups of samples [@{feranchuk2018evaluating}]. In this work the dependence of a parameter or of a positioning index by the taxonomic level $L$ is explicitly indicated in the corresponding symbol with the subscript '\@L', thus allowing a compact formal description of the microbial composition and diversity indices at every level. In particular, the following taxonomy levels will be considered: phylum ($L=1$), class ($L=2$), order ($L=3$), family ($L=4$), genus ($L=5$), species ($L=6$) and sequence variant (SV) or OTU ($L=SV$).

## Binomial model  {#sec:BinMod}

Let us consider a vector of abundances $\mathbf{a}=[a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{i},...,a_{\widehat{F}}]$ with $i=1,...,\widehat{F}$ 
<!-- of  $\widehat{F}$  features  -->
that represents the outcome of the sequencing of a single sample $S$. The element $a_i$ is the abundance of the $i$--th feature, $F_i$, and the sum of all features abundance is $R$ is the total library size, i.e. $R=\sum_{i=1}^{\widehat{F}}{a_i}$. This value depends on the assay settings and not on the input material thus is an arbitrary value characterizing the sequencing process and related to the sample richness [@quinn2018understanding]. In particular, the greater the value of R, the greater the coverage of less abundant features and therefore the greater the number of detected features, $\widehat{F}$, which tends to the actual number of features of the sequenced sample, $F$. The arbitrariness of $R$ means that counts of NGS data are not absolute but compositional and that can be modeled using the binomial distribution as follows: $a_i$ is the number of times a read has been successfully recognized as feature $F_i$ in $R$ independent sequencing reads with success probability equal to $p_i$, i.e. $a_i \sim \text{Bin}(R,p_i)$.
<!-- , with constraint $\sum_{i_1}^{F}{p_i}=1$.  -->
Within this model, a failure corresponds to the event that the sequenced read is not recognized as $F_i$ and has probability $q_i=(1-p_i)$. The support of the distribution is the set $\{0,1,...,R\}$. 


Although arbitrary, after sequencing the $R$ parameter is known and the proportion of successes of each observed feature, $\widehat{p}_i=\frac{a_i}{R}$, is an unbiased estimate of the corresponding binomial probability with variance equal to $Var\{\widehat{p}_i\}=\frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{R}$, thus library size affects precision of the relative abundance estimate.

Please note that features with null-probability can never be present in the sequencing result of a single sample since $p_i=0$ means that the feature is certainly absent from the sample and therefore will never be sequenced. Thus, all observed features have $a_i > 0$. Missing features counts occur only when at least two samples are analyzed simultaneously as some features may be unobserved in one of the sequenced samples. In this case, a-priori knowledge is needed to determine whether the corresponding missing count is due to the zero value of the sample feature probability or to the small number of sequenced reads that fail to ensure a reliable estimate of the binomial proportion. Missing counts must be properly managed based on the required analysis.

<!-- In any observed data set or sample there is the possibility, especially with low-probability events and with small data sets, of a possible event not occurring. Its observed frequency is therefore zero, apparently implying a probability of zero. This oversimplification is inaccurate and often unhelpful, -->
<!-- By artificially adjusting the probability of rare (but not impossible) events so those probabilities are not exactly zero, zero-frequency problems are avoided. Also see Cromwell's rule. -->
<!-- The simplest approach is to add one to each observed number of events, including the zero-count possibilities. This is sometimes called Laplace's rule of succession. This approach is equivalent to assuming a uniform prior distribution over the probabilities for each possible event (spanning the simplex where each probability is between 0 and 1, and they all sum to 1). -->
<!-- Pseudocounts should be set to one only when there is no prior knowledge at all – see the principle of indifference. However, given appropriate prior knowledge, the sum should be adjusted in proportion to the expectation that the prior probabilities should be considered correct, despite evidence to the contrary – see further analysis. Higher values are appropriate inasmuch as there is prior knowledge of the true values (for a mint-condition coin, say); lower values inasmuch as there is prior knowledge that there is probable bias, but of unknown degree (for a bent coin, say). -->

Unfortunately, in practice many ecologists have not been too concerned that classical diversity indices may give results that are misleading or difficult to interpret [59]. In their view, the actual values of the indices are unimportant, as long as they can be used to calculate the statistical significance of the change in diversity following a disturbance [46]. But in many cases this is not a reasonable basis for study conclusions, since the statistical significance of a change in the diversity index often has little to do with the actual magnitude or ecological significance of the change [52]. Furthermore, one index may indicate a statistically significant change in diversity while another index does not. [@daly2018ecological] 7.2. Estimators of Diversity Indices
7.2.1. Richness
Estimates of richness are obviously strongly correlated with the size of the sample used to obtain them: the total number of species in a sampling unit increases with its area and the number of detected individuals, and therefore comparing two different sampling units will be subject to bias. To address this, methods have been proposed that reduce samples of different sizes to a single standard size, so that they may be comparable in terms of their richness, a procedure known as rarefaction [55]. In sum, when one is faced with the task of selecting a diversity index, it is enlightening to consider Baumgärtner’s observation that all diversity indices require, to a greater or lesser extent, that the user makes a priori value judgements about which aspects of biodiversity are more important [13]. This includes, for example, the choice of the sensitivity parameter q in parametric families of indices. In choosing the value of q, the user specifies whether rare or common species are more important for the type of diversity they wish to study. Hints about the most appropriate value(s) to study might be gleaned from other insights into the community, but q cannot itself be measured or inferred from the community. Hence, there is no correct value of q in any application, and it must instead be chosen by the user based on the goals of the study.

# Sentence

Differential abundance analysis is controversial throughout microbiome research. Gold standard approaches require laborious measurements of total microbial load, or absolute number of microorganisms, to accurately determine taxonomic shifts. Therefore, most studies rely on relative abundance data. Here, we demonstrate common pitfalls in comparing relative abundance across samples and identify two solutions that reveal microbial changes without the need to estimate total microbial load. We define the notion of “reference frames”, which provide deep intuition about the compositional nature of microbiome data. In an oral time series experiment, reference frames alleviate false positives and produce consistent results on both raw and cell-count normalized data. Furthermore, reference frames identify consistent, differentially abundant microbes previously undetected in two independent published datasets from subjects with atopic dermatitis. These methods allow reassessment of published relative abundance data to reveal reproducible microbial changes from standard sequencing output without the need for new assays. 

Statistically convergent estimates of the diversity of major species (defined as those that together are covered by 95% of reads) can be achieved at the sample sizes of 10000 to 15000 reads. The relative error of the Shannon index estimate for this condition is lower than 4%. [@bukin2019effect] Modern microbiome studies often rely on the analysis of 16S ribosomal RNA sequences for the taxonomic identification of bacterial and archaeal strains. This kind of analysis has become a de factostandard for prokaryotic taxonomy. The 16S rRNA gene is approximately 1600 base pairs long and includes nine hypervariable regions of varying conservation (V1-V9). More conservative regions are
useful for determining the higher-ranking taxa, whereas more quickly evolving ones can help identify genus or species. Metabarcoding using 16S rRNA marker is widespread in the studies of various microbial communities.

The introduction of the next-generation sequencing techniques has led to novel applications of metabarcoding methods. In particular, increased read counts have allowed for quantitative estimates of the microbial community composition. Another advantage of NGS-based metabarcoding is that quantitative analysis has become available for communities of uncultured microbes. Yet, using NGS technologies has its limitations, caused chiefly by shorter read length. Its most important impact is the decreased precision of
species identification. The microbiome of lake Baikal is well-studied by microbiologists. Specifically, metabarcoding works have been performed for the communities of the
water column15–17, bottom sediments18–22, and communities associated with certain baikalian
organisms23,24. These works have shown that the bacterial biodiversity in the lake is extremely high.
High biodiversity in Lake Baikal can be explained by the presence of multiple distinct niches varying in
terms of environmental conditions.


Often, data on the abundances of the organisms are summarized by an index,
 such as a diversity measure. Changes in the community are then associated with changes
 in the measure. Although the measures used to assess such changes are subject to criticism
 (Hendrickson, 1979; Hurlbert, 1971), this approach is commonly used.
 [@smith1984nonparametric] 


Diversity is a concept central to ecology, and its measurement is essential for any study of
ecosystem health. But summarizing this complex and multidimensional concept in a single measure
is problematic. Dozens of mathematical indices have been proposed for this purpose, but these can
provide contradictory results leading to misleading or incorrect conclusions about a community’s
diversity. In this review, we summarize the key conceptual issues underlying the measurement of
ecological diversity, survey the indices most commonly used in ecology, and discuss their relative
suitability. We advocate for indices that: _{i} satisfy key mathematical axioms; (ii) can be expressed as
so-called effective numbers; (iii) can be extended to account for disparity between types; (iv) can be
parameterized to obtain diversity profiles; and (v) for which an estimator (preferably unbiased) can
be found so that the index is useful for practical applications. [@daly2018ecological] Any meaningful study of biodiversity, no matter which aspect is in question, must involve its
quantitative measurement. This is a complex task both conceptually and practically. Biodiversity is
quantified by constructing mathematical functions generally known as diversity indices. The use of
such indices permits comparisons between different spatial regions, temporal periods, taxa (species),
functional groups, or trophic levels. These measures are therefore essential tools for ecological
monitoring and conservation, as well as for any efforts to study and address the biodiversity crisis [6].  In recent years, the era of “Big Data”
has spread to ecology, in particular microbial ecology. This has driven a reassessment of which
diversity indices to use to summarize and analyze these data [7]. This has led to increased focus on
the mathematical behaviour of different measures, since there has been an increasing recognition
that ecologists (often non-experts in mathematics) are using measures of diversity without proper
consideration of their behaviour and limitations. This has led to difficulties in interpreting studies,
and especially in comparing them. As we shall see, the choice of index is highly dependent on the
particular study context. But there are a number of important points to consider. First and most importantly, ‘biodiversity’ is such a broad concept that it can and has been defined
in many different ways, depending on researchers’ specific needs and interests It is also clear that different diversity indices can therefore
measure patently different aspects of diversity. But even once researchers have decided which form of
 diversity they wish to measure, quantifying biodiversity is still problematic because there is no single
index that can provide a suitable summary. A second problem is the fact that the concept of diversity is often confounded with the indices
that measure it. Analogously, the most
commonly used diversity measure, the Shannon index, is actually a measure of entropy. Entropy refers
to uncertainty in information: Third, indices typically condense all relevant information about an ecosystem’s diversity into
a single real number, so that there are unfathomably many ways of calculating such an index
from the complex and extensive data on the ecosystem in question. Different indices can weigh
different components of these data more strongly than others, and can even entirely neglect some [13].
Needless to say, this freedom of formulation has permitted the emergence of dozens of different indices,
which often provide wildly different estimates of ostensibly the same quantity . A final confounding issue is the relatedness but non-equivalence of the concept of diversity across
different scientific disciplines. The obvious similarities between diversity measurement in, for example,
sociology or economics compared to ecology, have encouraged the adoption of indices by one field
from another, thus swelling their number without proper consideration of their conceptual differences. Before we delve further into ecological diversity and its mathematical representations, it is
important to emphasize that none of the numerous diversity indices are wrong per se. On the contrary,
each index has its own unique properties that are useful for specific applications. The key point of
Hurlbert’s criticism relates to diversity as a unified concept: since raw diversity indices exhibit such a
wide variety of mathematical behaviours, they cannot all give reasonable results when directly inserted
into any general equation or formula of diversity [8]. Thus it is critically important to consider the
purpose for which an index will be used, when addressing how it is constructed mathematically and
how it should be interpreted ecologically. The purpose of an index’s use will of course depend strongly on the context of the study. Examples
might include: classifying shifts in diversity after a disturbance; ranking ecosystems in terms of their
biodiversity (to determine which are more in need of protection); detecting the effects of external
(typically anthropogenic) factors on diversity; understanding interactions between diversity at different
trophic levels (i.e., how changes in one can affect another); or searching for mechanistic explanations
of diversity changes [6]. For each of these goals and many others, some indices will be more suitable
than others, and a poor choice may lead to misleading or even false conclusions. 

Components of diversity


It is generally understood that diversity can be divided into three components: richness, evenness,
and disparity [10]. Most indices (including almost all the classical and best established indices) do not
account for disparity, and hence this component of diversity is often neglected in reviews of the topic.
In this section, we provide definitions of these three components (illustrated in Figure 1), as well as a
brief summary of their ecological significance. 

Richness
In ecological terms, increased richness has been shown to both enhance community functionality
(i.e., increase productivity) and to stabilize it in the face of disturbances [21,22]. Two mechanisms are
believed to drive this effect [23]. The complementarity mechanism assumes that different species use
different resources, even if only slightly. Then communities with higher richness will use more of the
available resources, thus increasing their productivity. On the other hand, the selection mechanism
assumes that different species contribute differently to the community’s overall functionality,
namely that some species are more productive than others. Then richer communities are more
likely to contain more productive species, enhancing the community productivity

Of course, in practice ecologists can only count those species that they can find: rarely do they
encounter communities that can be fully censused, for obvious practical reasons. Instead, the richness
of a community must often be estimated from a sample or subset of the community, a topic that will be
discussed in Section 7.
Evenness
Aside from the total number of species in a community, the distribution of their abundances is also
an important component of diversity. If a species is represented by only a few individuals, it should
be clear that it contributes less to the community’s diversity than a species represented by several
thousand individuals. The equitability of a community’s species abundance distribution is referred
to as its evenness. A community is perfectly even if every species is present in equal proportions,
and uneven if one species dominates the abundance distribution.
The important role of species evenness in ecological diversity has received less attention than
that of species richness, but is also inarguable [24]. Evenness has been shown to be a key factor in
preserving the functional stability of ecosystems [25], as well as in enhancing productivity by increasing
the representation of each species’ functional traits [26]. In contrast, uneven communities are often
more susceptible to invasion and less resilient to stresses and disturbances [27].
Unlike richness, there is no consensus on how to measure evenness. The literature relating to the
formulation and choice of an evenness index is a self-contained and well-developed sub-field of the
diversity index literature. This topic is more narrowly focused, since it only considers one component of
diversity, and thus we restrict ourselves here to a short summary of the most important considerations
relating to evenness, and mention several extensive reviews of this topic for the interested reader.

Disparity
As we will shortly see, most classical diversity indices account for two components of
diversity—richness and evenness—and thus implicitly assume that distinct species have nothing
in common. That is to say, they do not account for any disparity between species. This conception of
diversity is referred to as species-neutral diversity [19]. It implies, for instance, that a community of six
dramatically different species is considered to be no more diverse than a community of six species
of butterflies.
Hence there are relatively fewer diversity indices that reflect the more realistic and nuanced
situation of varying dissimilarities between species. Such indices are termed similarity-sensitive.
The reason for the dearth of similarity-sensitive indices may well be the fact that “theoretical ecologists
have been hesitant to introduce new diversity indices when the profusion of similarity insensitive
indices is already perceived to form an impenetrable jungle” [36].

o account for species disparity, similarity-sensitive indices incorporate in their formulation some
measure of similarity. Many scientific fields make use of similarity measures, for example in biology
for taxonomic classification, in economics for analyzing investment policy, in information theory for
document filtering, or in genetics for sequence analysis [38]. A similarity measure is related in a
complementary way to the mathematical concept of a distance metric, since dissimilarity can often
be represented as a distance. However, many ecological dissimilarity measures do not fulfill all the
properties necessary to be considered a distance metric [19], and hence cannot make use of the many
theorems and results developed by mathematicians relating to distance metrics.
Within ecology, various methods for measuring similarity between species have already been
developed. Some are genetic [39], others are functional [40], taxonomic [41], morphological [42],
or phylogenetic [43]. They generally associate with each focal species some data concerning the
characteristics deemed to be important, such as a list of functional traits, a DNA sequence, a location
on a phylogenetic tree, and so on. The similarity values are then computed in terms of some notion of
difference between the associated data, depending on its particular characteristics

If the abundances are measured by
counting individuals, then the relative abundance pi represents the probability of randomly selecting
an individual of species i from amongst all individuals in the community. If the abundances are
measured in terms of biomass, then the relative abundance pi represents the relative share of the
community’s biomass that is stored in individuals of species i.

The richness of the community is simply S, while its evenness is calculated from the vector
of relative abundances p = (p1, ..., pS). Calculating the disparity additionally requires a similarity
measure, which we discuss later in Section 5.
The most commonly assumed axioms that a diversity index H(p) should satisfy are also common
to entropy measures, and are as follows [46]

5.1. Classical Indices
5.1.1. Definitions
The most widely used diversity indices can account for richness and evenness, but do not account
for species disparity. Instead they take as input the vector of relative abundances p = (p1, ..., pS),
where S is the total number of species in the community. Thus these indices measure species-neutral
diversity (see Section 3.3) and are known as classical diversity indice

5.1.2. Issues with Classical Indices
The most widely used measures of diversity in ecology are species richness, the Shannon index
and the Simpson index [59]. Together, they provide a perfect example of the problems discussed in
Sections 2 and 3: each index may be used to compare different communities to each other (although we
shall discuss shortly why even this can be problematic), but diversity values of the different indices
cannot be directly compared to each other. This is because each index has a different fundamental
meaning in terms of the diversity it measures.
Richness is simply the number of species in a community, the Simpson index represents the
probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to the same species, and the Shannon index
is a measure of the entropy or disorder of the community. These three indices measure conceptually
different features of a community, and hence have different units: richness is in units of species,
the Simpson index is a probability, and the Shannon index is an entropy measure, and therefore has
units of bits of information.
Thus, diversity measurements calculated using different classical indices are not immediately
comparable, which is a serious drawback for any scientific study. But even measurements calculated
using the same index can present important issues of comparison.

Diversity analysis using classical indices also suffers from their occasionally extreme non-linearity.


Unfortunately, in practice many ecologists have not been too concerned that classical diversity
indices may give results that are misleading or difficult to interpret [59]. In their view, the actual values
of the indices are unimportant, as long as they can be used to calculate the statistical significance of the
change in diversity following a disturbance [46]. But in many cases this is not a reasonable basis for
study conclusions, since the statistical significance of a change in the diversity index often has little to
do with the actual magnitude or ecological significance of the change [52]. Furthermore, one index
may indicate a statistically significant change in diversity while another index does not.

7. Practical Estimation of Diversity Indices
7.1. Background
When it comes to assessing the diversity of a community in practice, the species proportions
p = (p1, ..., pS) are generally unknown. Without a full census of the community, calculation of its
diversity using an index is not possible. Instead, this must be estimated from sampled data.
For the purpose of this discussion, we assume that we have a sample of n individuals from
the community in question. Most estimators of diversity assume that this sample is random,
namely that its observations are independent and identically distributed [94]. But this requires either
an infinite population, or sampling with replacement. Generally, neither of these requirements are met:
populations are finite and ecological studies typically sample populations without replacement [95].
This issue is avoided by considering a sample size much smaller than the population size, so that
the effect of sampling without replacement from a finite population can be neglected [96]. Thus the
problem reduces to estimating p using an appropriate sampling design, and then estimating the index
as a function of the estimated species abundance vector.
A good estimator of a diversity index is one that is unbiased and with minimal variance [19].
Therefore, an appropriate measure of an estimator’s error is the mean squared error (MSE), which is
the sum of squares of the bias and the variance [97]. Bias generally arises for two reasons: unobserved
species (those present in the community but not in the sample), and the non-linearity of indices with
respect to the species abundances. The former source of bias is exacerbated the more strongly the
index depends on S, the richness of the community. Hence, for example, the bias of the Simpson index
(Equation (8)) is less than that of the Shannon entropy (Equation (7)) since the former assigns less
weight to rare species, which are less likely to be sampled.
As with the indices themselves, their estimators should be selected carefully to ensure that
their formulation is appropriate for the particular application. Interrogation of this point is key,
particularly since non-experts often resort to dedicated statistical software or packages whose

underlying and disparate estimation techniques can result in different calculations of the same
quantity [7].
For most diversity indices, numerous estimators exist. The statistical details of their derivation
and bias reduction are beyond the scope of this review, so in this section we do not aim for an
in-depth discussion of these various estimators, but we instead focus on whether an unbiased
estimator exists for a particular index, and point the interested reader towards more exhaustive
reviews. Unbiased estimators are of course preferable to biased estimators, but in practice many
techniques exist for reducing bias, often to minimal levels, so that good estimates of diversity can still
be obtained with a biased index estimator.

7.2. Estimators of Diversity Indices
7.2.1. Richness
Estimates of richness are obviously strongly correlated with the size of the sample used to obtain
them: the total number of species in a sampling unit increases with its area and the number of detected
individuals, and therefore comparing two different sampling units will be subject to bias. To address
this, methods have been proposed that reduce samples of different sizes to a single standard size,
so that they may be comparable in terms of their richness, a procedure known as rarefaction [55].

The two most frequently used richness estimators are the Chao estimators (Chao1 and Chao2) [98,99],
and the jackknife method [95]. The Chao estimators estimate the number of unobserved species based
on the number of species that are observed either once or twice. The jackknife method is based on
resampling, and aims to reduce the estimator’s bias by considering subsets of the sample, which are
obtained by removing a certain number of observations (this number is known as the order of the
jackknife method).
7.2.2. Simpson Index
Simpson [57] provided an unbiased estimator of his own index (Equation (8)), which is based on
the number of pairs of individuals drawn without replacement:
7.2.3. Shannon Index
Due to its importance in numerous scientific fields, the Shannon entropy (Equation (7)) has seen
the development of many different estimators (Marcon [19] provides an overview). The details of these
estimators are beyond the scope of this review, but for our purposes we note that the estimation of the
Shannon index is subject to more bias than the estimation of Simpson’s index, since the former is more
sensitive to richness, i.e., to the number of species that are sampled.

This includes, for example, the choice of the sensitivity parameter q in

 Diversity indices
merely provide a summary of an inherently complex and multidimensional concept: a community’s
structure. Indices achieve this summarization in different ways by emphasizing different aspects of
diversity. To avoid confusion and misinterpretation, users should first define their objectives and then
choose the appropriate measure for the specific problem.
